A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Retained material can be matched across the conference reformatting and appendix renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original distillation experiments on Synth, CIFAR100 and SUB, including classification accuracy, representational similarity and concept recovery in Tables 1–4.

after.justification: V3 retains these original experiments and additionally reports a student-dimension ablation and an empirical illustration of the canonical-correlation bound.

M1.justification: The model family, centered-logit construction, L1/L2 distillation objectives and linear identifiability dissimilarity are unchanged. The added student-dimension sweep evaluates existing methods under different model configurations.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Synth, CIFAR100 and SUB for classification, representational alignment and concept recovery. The added analyses use retained datasets; Appendix H adds a mathematical counterexample, and language-model experiments remain future work.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparison methods remain KL-, L1- and L2-students with teacher references. Newly discussed similarity measures and distillation literature do not introduce evaluated competitors.

E3.justification: V3 adds a SUB protocol varying student dimension from 2 to 10 against a dimension-10 teacher, evaluating mCCA over the most aligned student-sized teacher subspace. It also evaluates the CIFAR bound at epochs 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50. The original experiments retain their stated splits, architectures and training budgets.

E4.justification: V3 adds two substantive analyses absent from v1: the SUB dimension ablation tests how student capacity affects label accuracy, concept recovery and alignment (Appendix L.1, Figure 8), while the CIFAR checkpoint analysis tests the empirical behavior of Theorem F.1's bound (Appendix F.5, Figure 3). These substantially expand the targeted evaluation beyond fixed-configuration comparisons.

E5.justification: The original five-teacher, five-student-seed reporting and inverse-variance aggregation are retained. V3 separately specifies one teacher and five student seeds for the dimension ablation, reporting means and standard deviations, and displays five individual seed trajectories for the bound check. These are additional replication designs, not an increase in the original experiments' run counts.

E6.justification: Under unchanged reported settings, Table 4 revises SUB mCCA from 0.787 to 0.417 for KL, 0.996 to 0.993 for L1, and 0.997 to 0.994 for L2, retaining ±0.001. Table 2 likewise changes KL from 0.79 to 0.42. Figures 3 and 8 add bound-check and capacity-sweep findings; Appendix G adds KL values of 0.002 and 0.0017. The KL-alignment finding changes materially, although the reason for the score revisions is unspecified.

T1.justification: The central bounds and their proofs, including unequal-dimension Theorem F.1, are retained. V3 requires diversity of only one model in Theorem 2.2 and supplies its proof in Appendix C.1. Remark E.3 revises an example's constant and extends the tightness argument to Jensen–Shannon divergence. New Appendix H constructs models with maximal embedding and unembedding mCCA but different distributions.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: logit distance controls linear representational similarity and concept preservation, KL provides weak practical guarantees, and logit-based distillation better preserves teacher representations. Additional evidence and qualifications do not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: V3 substantially expands the applicability discussion. It explains that matching unlikely labels can transfer teacher noise, explicitly discusses unequal representation dimensions and large-model optimization, and clarifies the last-layer focus and exclusion of cross-modal comparisons. It also explains why maximal mCCA need not imply matching distributions and why linear-invariant similarity measures suit this identifiability perspective without being universally preferable.

D1.justification: The implementation sections match across v1 Appendix K and v3 Appendix L: architectures, preprocessing, learning rates, training epochs, batch sizes, software and drep subsampling are retained. Both versions provide the same code-access link.

R1.justification: Appendix A expands positioning against orthogonal Procrustes, RSA and CKA invariances, and discusses further model families and multi-view research. New citations also support discussion of rank ordering, calibration and steering in Section 4. The central relationship to prior identifiability work remains unchanged; publication updates of existing references are not new works.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. V3 adds explanatory passages, expands related work and limitations, introduces an Impact Statement and adds appendix subsections. Author presentation and citation formatting also change, without a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from a single-column manuscript to a two-column conference layout, with new headers, reflowed equations and relocated tables. V3 adds Figure 3's bound plot, Figures 6–7's counterexample and Figure 8's ablation panels. V1 Figures 3–4 are retained as v3 Figures 4–5.

improvement.justification: V3 provides useful additional evidence about student capacity and the theoretical bound, makes the identifiability argument more self-contained, and adds meaningful qualifications about noisy rare labels and applicability. These improve support and interpretation while leaving the central work intact. The gains remain limited by the single-teacher ablation and unexplained SUB mCCA revisions.
